\begin{document}
\title{Inequality and Social Contests}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction }


\noindent

The interactions between inequality and status motivations remain contested. Although a rising consumer attention to status goods has been widely critiqued (Veblen, 1899; Frank, 1985), the link between relative status and subjective well-being (Clark, Frijters \& Shields, 2008) makes it difficult to dismiss status motivations as socially wasteful. Therefore, status-related consumption is not merely a reflection of well-established hierarchies - but also a means to build and maintain social hierarchies.


Indeed the very notions of hierarchy are themselves subject to competing interpretations. Some have explained social hierarchy through unequal access to material resources and structural advantages (Kendall, 2002), while others emphasise upon reproduction of inequality through social networks, cultural knowledge, and norms (Weber, 1922). The current paper uses Weber’s (1922) framework of status groups and relies on Goode’s (1978) commentary on consumption as a mechanism of social mobility to situate status competitions within a closed economy of firms and labour. The economic interactions in the model treat social networks as an agent of adaptability of skills that are relevant in the economy - thereby considering economic role played by social networks.

More specifically, the participants in the closed economy invest in market-relevant adaptability -- such as skills, behavioural conformity, and professional signalling -- while a long-term social categorisation based on language, nationality, religion, or political identity evolves far more slowly and continues to shape trust, loyalty, also shape the perceived legitimacy of participants within the economy (Tilly, 1998; Bourdieu, 1986). The framework is then used to investigate the extent to which inequality may encourage positional competition and yet present indirect costs through lack of economic growth. The questions we're concerned with are i) how adaptability related expenditures (or social capital investments) respond to rise in inequality and ii) how inequality imposes limits of growth through constraints of social hierarchy. 

\newpage

\section{Model}
\noindent

At the core of the model is a dichotomy between two forms of social positioning: adaptability and long-term categorisation. Adaptability refers to short-term, market-driven traits such as skills, linguistic abilities, personality fit, and professional behaviour. Such traits are more often shaped by transactional interactions and can be improved through social capital investments influenced by economic incentives. Relative to such skills, the long-term categorisation, reflects slow-moving social identification including race, religion, political affiliation or nationality. These are shaped through non-transactional, contractual, and trust-based processes of social cohesion and assimilation, and evolve far more slowly than what falls in the realm of adaptability (Weber, 1922).

This dichotomy reflects a key dynamic in social life: individuals can readily adapt their behaviour to fit social and professional environments (e.g. the “chameleon effect”), but they also must remain constrained by social identities that shape how they interact in a social environment. While firms and institutions rely on adaptability to generate revenue, they also operate within broader social environments where long-term categorisation influences trust, loyalty, and stability.

A model for economy integrates the dichotomy using a framework of labour-queue theory (Spence). More particularly, we consider firms must rank workers based on the perceived earning potentials of workers. While the higher rank of an employee may depend on both adaptability and categorisation, the firm's revenue based planning -- which deals more often with short-term pressures -- can only consider workers' adaptability investments. An asymmetry thus follows -- workers invest in both dimensions of social capital: adaptability to enhance short-term productivity and categorisation to secure long-term social positioning -- but firms can only account for adaptability.

The model is operationalised as a three-player game involving a firm and two workers competing in a labour queue (see Section \ref{sec:closed_economy}). The three-game formulation itself is a stylised view of a more general $N$-player economy where workers compete for positions with both social capital investments and social lottery (see Appendix for details). 

\subsection{Labour and Firm}\label{sec:closed_economy}

\noindent

Drawing on a Schumpeterian closed economy, we assume that all income circulates between workers and firm. The economic growth arises from continual introductions of new or higher-quality goods. Workers supply labour and receive wages -- which in turn become the domestic demand. Firms use the revenue generated from this demand -- either directly through consumer investment in skills or profit -- to fund innovation. Successful innovation produces new product and improves existing services -- generating the next round of income. This circular flow of wages, consumption, and innovation creates an endogenous engine of growth: consumption completes one innovation cycle by returning income to firms, while investment initiates the next by financing the search for new products. In long-run equilibrium that follows, the firms choose an optimal allocation of resources that sustains a steady stream of innovation and revenues.

In the three player simplification, the high-performing and low-performing workers choose an optimal combination of skill investment and the investment in the lottery of social mobility, whereas firms set training costs and wage differentials to maximise asset value net of depreciation as well as asset-maintenance costs. While labour sorting is under firm's control, the social costs -- such as job search costs for workers, or influence of social networks -- act as constraints for the firm. The asymmetry between workers and firm is reflected in the fact that while firms capture the returns to innovation and skill formation, the costs of building durable social ties — rooted in long-term categorisation processes — are borne by workers and do not feed back into firm's revenues.


\subsection{Model Dynamics}\label{sec:firmbehaviour}

\noindent

The choice for workers in the economy is represented as a reference-dependent S-shaped utility function. As detailed in the Appendix, this is implied by an $N$-player formulation of competitions where workers use both social lottery and upskilling in a fixed socio-economic ladder. In the stylised view -- consisting of two workers and a firm -- the workers choose a certain mixing criterion $\lambda$ to distribute income between fixed-lottery benefit $\Lambda$ (of cost $L$) and the upskilling costs or the social capital investments. The lottery benefit $\Lambda$ is an exogenous benefit from social connections that is not managed by the firm. We further assume that the training costs charged to consumer are part of exogenous maintenance costs of assets so that all what firm can do in order to maximise its profit in the economy is to adjust the pay-distribution ($\alpha$) among the two-workers. 

More formally, the firm only controls: 
\begin{enumerate}

\item  $\alpha$ --  the firm chooses $0 < \alpha < \frac{1}{2} $  so that the higher-rank (top-performer) worker is given $1-\alpha$ as wage while the lower-rank (bottom-of-the-queue performer) worker is given $\alpha$ as wage
\end{enumerate}

The differences in choice of the two workers arise solely due to the reference-dependent S-shaped utility curve. In other words, the two workers make different choices for their share of wage spent on social capital investments. The two different selections of mixing variables are:

\begin{enumerate}
\item $\lambda$ -- portion of wage spent on adaptability by lower-ranked worker
\item $\eta$ --  portion of wage spent on adaptability by higher-ranked worker
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Choice for Firm}

\noindent

The growth of firm's assets is subject to asset-maintenance costs $C(A)$ and a constant depreciation $\delta$.  The depreciation of assets means that firm are forced to rely on investments from the worker while the asset-maintenance costs pose limits on a steady growth in assets through income addition alone \footnote{All efficiency loss in collection of investments from workers are considered as part of asset-maintaining costs.}. In the long-term equilibrium, a firm chooses $\alpha$ so that the income stream balances the decline in assets and asset-maintenance costs.

Assuming a constant depreciation $\delta$ on accumulated $A_t$, the firm distributes a fixed proportion $\kappa$ of  $A_t$ as wage - while the rest of $A_t(1-\kappa)$ contributes to maintaining or incrementing existing assets. Out of $R_t\equiv \kappa A_t $ that needs to be distributed as wages, the firm provides $\alpha R_t$ to the lower rank worker and $(1-\alpha)R_t$ to the higher rank worker. 

For the low-rank worker's choice of $\lambda_t$, the amount $\alpha R_t \lambda_t$ is spent in adaptability and for the higher-rank worker's choice of $\eta_t$, $(1-\alpha)R_t \eta_t$ is spent on adaptability. The total contribution $\psi_t = R_t (\lambda_t \alpha+ (1-\alpha)\eta_t)$ thus flows back to the firm as upskilling investments (workers' expenditure). 

Other than the depreciation $\delta A_t$, the assets at any given time incur two additional costs

\begin{enumerate}
\item the operational costs with the distribution of $R_t = \kappa A_t$ to workers as well as the collection costs for workers' contribution $\psi_t $ -- represented as a (power) cost-function  $K(\alpha)$ 
\item the maintenance cost for assets $(1-\kappa)A_t$ -- represented as a cost-function $C(A_t)$
\end{enumerate}

The firm thus chooses $\alpha$ in order to maximise $A_{t+1}$ for a given $A_t$ at every cycle -- with the following dynamics 

\begin{align*}
A_{t+1}=(1-\kappa-\delta) A_t + \kappa A_t (\lambda_t \alpha + (1-\alpha)\eta_t) - K(\alpha) - C(A_t)
\end{align*}

For a fixed $\lambda_t$ and $\eta_t$, the firm does benefit from lowering $\alpha$ since that would imply a high collection $(1-\alpha)$ despite lower operational costs (less distribution). In other words, the firm benefits from lower pay so long as $\eta_t$ is high and $(1-\alpha)\eta_t$ is significant. The next section explores whether this asymmetry between $\eta_t$ and $\lambda_t$ can persist in equilibrium or not.


\subsubsection{Choice for Workers}

\noindent


With a fixed subjective benefit $\Lambda$ from the lottery for either workers, the lower-rank worker optimises the following utility 

\begin{align*}
u(\lambda_t) \equiv \upsilon(\alpha R_t \lambda_t) +\Lambda \frac{\alpha R_t(1-\lambda_t)}{\alpha R_t(1-\lambda_t) + (1-\alpha) R_t(1-\eta_t)}
\end{align*}

Similarly, the higher-rank worker optimises the following utility

\begin{align*}
U(\eta_t) \equiv \upsilon((1-\alpha) R_t \eta_t)  + \Lambda \frac{(1-\alpha) R_t(1-\eta_t)}{\alpha R_t(1-\lambda_t)+(1-\alpha) R_t(1-\eta_t)}
\end{align*}

The solutions for both can be found explicitly for $\upsilon(x)\equiv x$ and implicitly (numerical solution) using $\upsilon(x)\equiv \sqrt{x}$.

\section*{Appendix}


\subsection*{The closed $N$-player economy } \label{sec:nplayereconomy}

\noindent


The stylised model for workers relies on the dynamics implied by an $N$-player economy where both social lottery and training costs suggest a separation of workers based on risks in the closed economy. In the microeconomic formulation of the endoegnous growth economy, the stratified labour is represented as fixed ladder of jobs occupied by workers at any given point in time. Each position in the ladder is associated with a distinct income level that is eventually set by the firm. Every worker holds exactly one job and the number of jobs does not change over time in the economy. While we assume no long-term unemployment, the workers in the economy face temporary job loss \footnote{The technological changes or internal reorganization that lead to such losses circusmscribe the creative destruction in endogenous growth economy.}. Upon the job-loss, the worker faces the choice to re-enter the job-market with costs of up-skilling and play a lottery to swap the current position with someone else in the job-market.

In other words, a displaced worker can return to the previous job by investing in the skills or certifications required to perform it. Since higher-ranked jobs with higher-income require greater skill, the upward move requires substantial retraining costs. The retraining costs are forgone by the worker in accepting lower-ranked jobs. Mobility thus occurs through three mechanisms i) voluntary movement down the ladder ii) costly investment to move upward iii) or a lottery for positions among other workers.

The model captures these possibilities with the three choices. The worker may  (i) swap her job with a lower-ranked worker who is willing to acquire the skills necessary to move up (therefore paying the price to move up) (ii) pay the skill cost required to claim a higher-ranked position from someone willing to step down, or (iii) pay a fixed cost that provides mobility with some risk (social lottery). Such options reflect different mechanisms of job mobility - training, competition, and luck.

The set up of the model also entails a variation of risk across incomes. More specifically, the higher-income positions have greater training requirements (factoring in a longer search time and other costs arising out of short-term unemployment) and thus a higher acquisition cost. Since workers in high-skill, high-income positions face greater absolute losses when displaced, the risk of income loss in absolute terms increases with higher income-levels. With all workers having the same preferences, the differences in behaviour across income levels are driven by well-known pattern of risk-aversion for small-gains and higher risk-taking for higher losses. This is captured by the model with an S-shaped Friedman-Savage utility for the worker.



Formally, the set up the model includes the following conditions. 
\begin{enumerate}

\item The choice for the worker is to either pay cost-of-upskilling or use the social lottery to move up the economic ladder. The lottery is of a fixed cost $L$ so that another worker $k$ out of N workers is randomly selected to swap her job with worker $i$. Worker $k$ does not pay any additional cost other than the fixed lottery cost $L$ for such a swap.

\item If not playing the lottery, a worker with income $m_i$  may take up a job that pays $m_{k}$ so long as the worker pays a transition-cost $C(m_i,m_{k})$ -- a power-cost-function defined as follows 

\[
C(m_i,m_k) =
\begin{cases}
(m_k - m_i)^b, & \text{for } m_i > m_k \\
0,            & \text{for } m_i < m_k
\end{cases}
\] Above ensures that $\forall {k\le i}$,  we have $C(m_i,m_{k})=0$ i.e. no cost is paid for moving from a position of high-skill to low (or the same) skill. Higher $b$ corresponds to higher costs (charged by the firm - as discussed in Section \ref{sec:firmbehaviour}).

\item The income-levels are specified with a single-parameter $a$ in the pareto income list $ x_0  (1 - i)^{-1 / a}$ for $1 \le i \le N$.  A higher $a$ corresponds to higher-stakes through income levels.

\end{enumerate}

The more a worker upskills oneself, the harder it becomes for the worker to move up (as the swap pool gets limited). A higher-income employee would also have less likelihood of being replaced (less transferrable-skills due to higher costs). The long-term transition-probability can thus be determined from the costs of moving up the ladder. 

It follows from the dynamics that in the long-term equilibrium, higher costs ($b$) discourage mobility and higher stakes ($a$) encourage bets.  The S-shaped utility means that in the long-term equilbrium, the higher-rank workers would prefer the downgrade while the low-rank workers may prefer the lottery.
